# Senate Confirms Mukasey as Attorney General Amid Waterboarding Debate

(CNN) -- Following weeks of contentious debate over Michael Mukasey's stance on waterboarding, the Senate voted late Thursday to confirm the former judge as attorney general, with a final tally of 53-40.

The interrogation technique had threatened to derail President Bush's nominee for the top post at the Justice Department. Bush had tapped Mukasey to succeed longtime confidant Alberto Gonzales, who stepped down in September. The nomination appeared imperiled after several Democratic senators raised objections stemming from Mukasey's ambiguous positions on waterboarding and on the extent of presidential authority to authorize electronic surveillance.

Mukasey, a former federal judge from New York, told senators he found waterboarding "repugnant" but stopped short of declaring definitively whether the practice constitutes torture—a designation prohibited under both American and international law. The technique involves restraining a subject while pouring water over the face to simulate the sensation of drowning.

Mukasey's path to confirmation became considerably clearer last week when two influential Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee—Sens. Dianne Feinstein of California and Chuck Schumer of New York—announced they would support his nomination despite the surrounding controversy.

"The Department of Justice, once the crown jewel among government institutions, is adrift and rudderless," Schumer remarked Tuesday, the same day the committee voted 11-8 to advance Mukasey's nomination to the full Senate. "It desperately needs a strong and independent leader at the helm to set it back on course, and I believe Judge Mukasey is that person."

Schumer recounted that during a Friday meeting, the nominee affirmed that Congress would be well within its constitutional authority to enact legislation banning waterboarding across all government agencies—and that the president "would have absolutely no legal authority to ignore" such a law. Schumer further expressed confidence that Mukasey would be more inclined than an interim attorney general to deem waterboarding unlawful. "Indeed, his written responses to our inquiries have demonstrated greater openness to ending the practices we abhor than either of this president's previous attorney general nominees."

Yet Mukasey's assurances failed to convince Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, chairman of the Judiciary Committee. "Some have sought to find comfort in Judge Mukasey's personal assurance that he would enforce a future, new law against waterboarding if this Congress were to pass one," Leahy said Tuesday. "Unsaid, of course, is the fact that any such prohibition would have to be enacted over the veto of this president."

Sen. Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania, the committee's ranking Republican, offered a more sanguine assessment, expressing confidence that Mukasey would faithfully enforce any law prohibiting waterboarding. "He could have said a lot of things which would have given me more assurances," Specter noted. "But he is intelligent; he's really learned in the law. He's strong, ethical, honest beyond any question. He's not an intimate of the president."

Public opinion on the matter remains divided, according to a poll released Tuesday. While a majority of Americans regard waterboarding as a form of torture, a notable segment nonetheless believes its use by the U.S. government is justified in certain circumstances. When asked whether waterboarding constitutes torture, 69 percent of respondents answered affirmatively, while 29 percent disagreed. When asked whether the government should be permitted to employ the technique to extract information from suspected terrorists, 58 percent said no and 40 percent said yes.

The CNN/Opinion Research Corp. telephone survey, which polled 1,024 American adults over the weekend, carries a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points.

The contentious issue had put the confirmation of President Bush's pick to head the Justice Department in jeopardy.

Bush had put forward Mukasey's name to succeed Alberto Gonzales, a close political ally who stepped down from the position in September. Prior to the vote, the confirmation looked uncertain, as several Democratic lawmakers balked at supporting Mukasey due to his ambiguous answers about waterboarding and about presidential authority regarding electronic surveillance without warrants.

During his testimony, Mukasey—who previously served as a federal judge in New York—described waterboarding as something he found "repugnant." Still, he stopped short of definitively classifying it as torture, a practice prohibited under both domestic and international legal standards. The technique itself involves holding down a subject while pouring water over their face to simulate the experience of drowning.

The path toward confirmation became considerably smoother last week when two influential Democratic members of the Senate Judiciary Committee—California's Dianne Feinstein and New York's Chuck Schumer—announced their intention to back Mukasey despite lingering concerns.

Schumer characterized the Justice Department's current state in stark terms on Tuesday, the same day the committee approved sending the nomination to the full Senate by an 11-8 vote. "The Department of Justice, once the crown jewel among government institutions, is adrift and rudderless," he remarked, adding that the agency required "a strong and independent leader at the helm to set it back on course" and expressing his belief that "Judge Mukasey is that person."

According to Schumer, during a private conversation on Friday, Mukasey acknowledged that Congress possesses the authority to enact legislation prohibiting waterboarding throughout government agencies, and that the president would lack any legal grounds to disregard such a law. Schumer suggested that Mukasey would likely be more inclined than a temporary attorney general to eventually deem waterboarding unlawful. He further noted that Mukasey's written responses revealed "more openness to ending the practices we abhor" compared to the president's two previous attorney general picks.

Not everyone found this assurance convincing, however. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, a Democrat from Vermont, dismissed the significance of Mukasey's promise to uphold any future anti-waterboarding legislation. "Some have sought to find comfort in Judge Mukasey's personal assurance that he would enforce a future, new law against waterboarding if this Congress were to pass one," Leahy stated Tuesday, pointing out that such a prohibition would inevitably require overriding a presidential veto to become law.

Pennsylvania's Arlen Specter, the committee's top-ranking Republican, expressed confidence that Mukasey would indeed uphold any such ban. "He could have said a lot of things which would have given me more assurances," Specter noted, "but he is intelligent; he's really learned in the law. He's strong, ethical, honest beyond any question. He's not an intimate of the president."

Public opinion on the matter appears divided, based on survey results released Tuesday. While a clear majority of Americans—69 percent—view waterboarding as a torture technique, opinions split on whether the government should be permitted to employ it against terrorism suspects: 58 percent opposed its use, while 40 percent supported allowing it. These findings emerged from a CNN/Opinion Research Corporation phone survey of 1,024 U.S. adults conducted over the preceding weekend, carrying a margin of error of 4.5 percentage points.

The United States Senate voted 53-40 to confirm Michael Mukasey as the nation's next attorney general, bringing to a close weeks of contentious debate centered largely on his refusal to explicitly condemn waterboarding as a form of torture. The confirmation vote marked the culmination of a nomination process that had grown increasingly uncertain amid mounting scrutiny from lawmakers concerned about executive power and interrogation practices.

President George W. Bush had originally put forward Mukasey, a retired federal judge from New York, to fill the vacancy left by Alberto Gonzales, who stepped down from the position in September. As a respected jurist with a reputation for independence, Mukasey was seen by the administration as a candidate capable of restoring credibility to a Justice Department that had been rocked by controversy under his predecessor.

Despite this reputation, Mukasey's path to confirmation was far from smooth. Several Democratic senators voiced serious reservations about his positions on two critical issues: the legality of waterboarding as an interrogation technique and the scope of presidential authority in matters of electronic surveillance. Central to their concerns was Mukasey's unwillingness to unequivocally label waterboarding as torture, a stance that many lawmakers viewed as an implicit endorsement of practices they considered unconstitutional or inhumane. This ambiguity threatened to derail his nomination entirely, as critics questioned whether he would adequately check executive overreach in his role as the nation's top law enforcement official.

The turning point came when two influential Democratic senators, Dianne Feinstein of California and Chuck Schumer of New York, announced their support for Mukasey's confirmation. Schumer, in particular, framed his decision around the pressing institutional needs of the Justice Department, arguing that the agency required steady and capable leadership after a period of turmoil. He also pointed to assurances he had received from Mukasey indicating that the nominee would respect and uphold any congressional legislation explicitly banning waterboarding across all government agencies, should such a law be enacted. This commitment appeared to alleviate some of the concerns that had initially made Democrats hesitant to support his nomination.

With this critical backing secured, the Senate Judiciary Committee moved forward, voting 11-8 to advance Mukasey's nomination to the full Senate for consideration. This committee vote proved to be a pivotal step, clearing the way for the broader Senate floor vote that ultimately resulted in his confirmation as attorney general, despite the divisions his nomination had exposed within Congress over issues of torture, executive authority, and the limits of presidential power in matters of national security.

Mukasey, a retired federal judge from New York, was nominated by President Bush to replace Alberto Gonzales, who resigned in August amid controversy over the firing of U.S. attorneys and questions about his credibility with Congress. Their support proved decisive in securing the votes needed for confirmation, as other Democrats remained divided on the nomination.

# CNN's Coverage After Hurricane Michael

When Hurricane Michael made landfall in October 2018, it left a trail of destruction across the Florida Panhandle that would dominate news cycles for weeks. CNN's coverage in the aftermath of this catastrophic storm exemplified the network's approach to disaster journalism, combining on-the-ground reporting with broader analysis of the human and economic toll.

## Immediate Response

In the hours and days after Michael struck, CNN deployed correspondents to hard-hit areas like Mexico Beach and Panama City, Florida. These journalists captured the raw devastation—flattened homes, uprooted trees, and communities struggling to comprehend the scale of destruction. The network's meteorologists had tracked the storm's rapid intensification, providing viewers with crucial warnings before it became one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the continental United States.

## Human Stories

Beyond the statistics and property damage assessments, CNN's reporting focused heavily on personal narratives. Stories emerged of survivors who had ridden out the storm in their homes, families separated during evacuation, and communities coming together to support one another. These human interest pieces helped audiences connect emotionally with a disaster occurring hundreds of miles away.

## Long-Term Coverage

What distinguished CNN's approach was its commitment to following the story well after the initial news cycle faded. The network returned to affected areas months later to document rebuilding efforts, the challenges of insurance claims, and the psychological toll on residents. This sustained attention highlighted issues often overlooked once major storms leave the headlines—the slow, difficult process of recovery that communities face long after cameras typically move on to the next story.

This pattern of coverage—immediate crisis reporting followed by extended follow-up—has become characteristic of how major news networks approach natural disasters, ensuring public attention doesn't simply vanish once the immediate danger passes.

**Senate Confirms Mukasey as Attorney General Despite Waterboarding Controversy**

*Vote comes after bruising battle over nominee's refusal to call interrogation technique torture*

WASHINGTON (CNN) — The Senate voted Thursday to confirm Michael Mukasey as the nation's 81st attorney general, ending a contentious confirmation battle that centered largely on the retired federal judge's refusal to explicitly state whether waterboarding constitutes torture.

The vote was 53-40, with several Democrats joining Republicans to approve President Bush's nominee to replace Alberto Gonzales, who resigned amid controversy over the firing of U.S. attorneys.

Mukasey's nomination had appeared in jeopardy in recent weeks after he repeatedly declined, during Senate Judiciary Committee hearings and in written follow-up responses, to characterize waterboarding — a technique that simulates drowning — as illegal torture. The judge told lawmakers he found the practice "repugnant" but said he could not offer a legal opinion without knowing the specific circumstances under which it might be used, citing concerns about exposing CIA interrogators to prosecution.

That answer infuriated many Democrats and human rights advocates, who argued that a nominee for the nation's top law enforcement position should be able to state unequivocally that waterboarding violates U.S. and international law.

"This is not a hard question," said Sen. Edward Kennedy, D-Massachusetts, who voted against confirmation. "Waterboarding is torture. It has been prosecuted as a war crime by the United States in the past. For the attorney general-designate to hedge on this issue raises serious doubts about his independence from this administration."

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, also opposed the nomination, saying Mukasey's answers left him unable to certify that the nominee would enforce the law without regard to White House pressure.

But other Senate Democrats, including Judiciary Committee members Chuck Schumer of New York and Dianne Feinstein of California, broke with colleagues to support Mukasey, arguing that the Justice Department could not afford to remain without permanent leadership and that Mukasey's reputation for independence outweighed concerns over the waterboarding issue.

"I have concerns, as many do, about his answers on interrogation techniques," Schumer said ahead of the vote. "But the department is adrift. It needs a strong, credible leader who is independent of the White House, and I believe Judge Mukasey is that person."

Feinstein echoed that sentiment, noting Mukasey's long record as a federal judge in New York, where he presided over terrorism cases including that of "Blind Sheikh" Omar Abdel-Rahman.

Republicans largely rallied behind the nominee, dismissing the waterboarding dispute as a distraction from more pressing concerns at a Justice Department still reeling from the U.S. attorneys scandal.

"Judge Mukasey is a man of unquestioned integrity, intellect, and independence," said Sen. Arlen Specter, R-Pennsylvania, the Judiciary Committee's ranking Republican. "The Senate would be wise not to let one issue, however important, obscure his obvious qualifications."

The White House praised the vote as a step toward restoring stability at the Justice Department. Press Secretary Dana Perino said President Bush looked forward to swearing in Mukasey "as soon as possible" so he could begin addressing what she called "the serious challenges facing the department."

Mukasey, 66, is expected to be sworn in within days. He inherits a department still under scrutiny from congressional investigators over the dismissal of nine U.S. attorneys last year — firings that critics alleged were politically motivated and that ultimately led to Gonzales's resignation in September.

In a statement issued after the vote, Mukasey thanked the Senate for its confidence and pledged to restore public trust in the department.

"The Department of Justice must enforce the law without fear or favor, and must be seen to do so," Mukasey said. "That will be my guiding principle."

Still, the waterboarding controversy is unlikely to fade quickly. Several senators who voted against Mukasey said Thursday they intend to press the new attorney general for clearer answers once he takes office, and Judiciary Committee Democrats have signaled they may seek additional documents from the CIA regarding the agency's use of the interrogation technique.

"This vote may be over," Leahy said, "but the questions it raised are not going away."

**WASHINGTON (AP)** — The Senate voted 53-40 Thursday to confirm Michael B. Mukasey as the nation's 81st attorney general, ending a contentious nomination battle that centered largely on the retired federal judge's refusal to explicitly declare the interrogation technique known as waterboarding illegal.

Mukasey, 66, was nominated by President George W. Bush in September to replace Alberto Gonzales, who resigned amid controversy over the firings of U.S. attorneys and other Justice Department scandals. He is expected to be sworn in within days.

The vote broke largely along party lines, though several Democrats crossed over to support the nominee, while a handful of Republicans joined the majority of Democrats in opposition.

The confirmation fight intensified in recent weeks after Mukasey, during his confirmation hearings, declined to state unequivocally whether waterboarding — a technique that simulates drowning — constitutes torture under U.S. law. That answer alarmed civil liberties advocates and many Democrats, who argued that the nation's chief law enforcement officer should be able to draw a clear line on the legality of the practice.

Sen. Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., who had recommended Mukasey to the White House and championed his nomination despite the waterboarding controversy, defended his support on the Senate floor.

"This was not an easy decision, and I understand the concerns my colleagues have raised," Schumer said. "But after the chaos and politicization we saw at the Justice Department under Attorney General Gonzales, we need a person of proven integrity and independence leading that department. Judge Mukasey is that person."

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, D-Vt., who voted against confirmation, said he could not overlook Mukasey's evasiveness on the torture question.

"The attorney general of the United States must be willing to say clearly that waterboarding is torture and is illegal," Leahy said. "I remain troubled that Judge Mukasey would not give a straight answer to a question with a clear answer. That is not the kind of leadership the Justice Department needs right now."

Sen. Arlen Specter, R-Pa., the committee's ranking Republican, urged colleagues to look past the waterboarding dispute and focus on what he called Mukasey's decades of distinguished service.

"Judge Mukasey has an unimpeachable record as a jurist and as a man of the law," Specter said. "The Justice Department has been without steady leadership for far too long. We owe it to the American people to confirm a qualified nominee and let him get to work restoring confidence in that institution."

The debate over Mukasey's nomination reflected broader tensions in Congress over the Bush administration's detention and interrogation policies in the years following the Sept. 11 attacks. Critics said the refusal to unambiguously condemn waterboarding raised questions about whether the incoming attorney general would adequately check executive branch authority on matters of national security.

Supporters countered that Mukasey, a former U.S. district judge in New York with a reputation for independence, was the best available choice to restore credibility to a department rocked by controversy.

With his confirmation secured, Mukasey now inherits a Justice Department still grappling with the fallout from the U.S. attorney firings and calls for greater transparency in decisions on detainee treatment and warrantless surveillance programs.

# The Controversial Confirmation of Michael Mukasey: Waterboarding Testimony and Public Opinion

When President George W. Bush nominated Michael Mukasey, a retired federal judge, to serve as Attorney General in September 2007, the confirmation process quickly became embroiled in one of the most contentious debates of the era: the legality and morality of waterboarding as an interrogation technique.

## Background on the Nomination

Mukasey was nominated to replace Alberto Gonzales, whose tenure as Attorney General had been marked by controversy over the firing of U.S. attorneys and the administration's legal justifications for controversial counterterrorism policies. Bush and his advisors hoped Mukasey's reputation as a respected jurist—having served on the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York—would provide a smoother confirmation process than his predecessor's tenure had been.

## The Waterboarding Controversy

During his Senate Judiciary Committee confirmation hearings in October 2007, Mukasey faced intense questioning about waterboarding, a technique that simulates drowning and had been used by the CIA on terrorism suspects during the Bush administration.

When pressed by senators to state definitively whether waterboarding constituted torture, Mukasey declined to give an unequivocal answer. He stated that he found the practice "repugnant" but said he could not determine whether it was illegal without knowing the specific circumstances under which it was used. This carefully hedged response drew sharp criticism from Democratic senators, who argued that a nominee for the nation's top law enforcement position should be able to clearly state that waterboarding—historically prosecuted as a war crime in other contexts—was illegal torture.

Senators including Edward Kennedy, Dianne Feinstein, and others expressed frustration that Mukasey's evasiveness suggested he might be unwilling to challenge the administration's aggressive interrogation policies. Some senators threatened to oppose his confirmation specifically because of this issue, since it raised concerns about whether he would enforce legal limits on executive branch interrogation practices.

## Public Opinion on Waterboarding

The controversy surrounding Mukasey's testimony coincided with broader public debate about waterboarding's legality and morality. Polling conducted around this period revealed a divided American public. Surveys generally showed that a majority of Americans considered waterboarding to be a form of torture, though opinions varied based on how questions were framed and whether they specifically addressed its use against terrorism suspects.

This division in public opinion mirrored the split in Congress. While some polls indicated public support for using aggressive interrogation techniques against suspected terrorists in specific circumstances, other surveys showed significant discomfort with waterboarding when it was explicitly labeled as torture—highlighting the same definitional ambiguity that made Mukasey's testimony so contentious.

## The Confirmation Outcome

Despite the controversy, Mukasey was ultimately confirmed by the Senate on November 8, 2007, by a vote of 53-40. Several senators who had expressed concerns about his waterboarding testimony ultimately voted to confirm him, citing his overall qualifications and judicial temperament, while others voted against confirmation specifically citing his refusal to condemn waterboarding as torture.

## Legacy of the Controversy

The Mukasey confirmation controversy became emblematic of the broader "torture debate" that characterized the Bush administration's later years. It highlighted the tension between legal officials' reluctance to make definitive statements that could expose government personnel to prosecution and the public's desire for clear ethical and legal standards regarding interrogation practices.

The controversy also foreshadowed continued debates about enhanced interrogation techniques that would persist into the Obama administration, which officially banned waterboarding, and would resurface again in subsequent political discussions about interrogation policy in later years.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The Senate voted Thursday to confirm Michael Mukasey as the nation's 81st attorney general, capping weeks of contentious debate over his refusal to explicitly classify the interrogation technique known as waterboarding as illegal torture.

The vote was 53-40, with several Democrats joining Republicans to approve President Bush's nominee despite concerns raised by members of both parties over Mukasey's testimony during confirmation hearings.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, ultimately voted against confirmation, citing what he called Mukasey's "troubling unwillingness to state clearly that waterboarding is illegal."

"This isn't a close call. It isn't a gray area," Leahy said on the Senate floor before the vote. "Waterboarding is torture, and it violates our laws and treaty obligations."

Mukasey, a retired federal judge, told lawmakers during his confirmation hearings that he found the practice of waterboarding -- which simulates drowning -- "repugnant," but stopped short of declaring it illegal, saying he had not been briefed on the classified details of the CIA's interrogation program.

"I don't know what's involved in the technique," Mukasey said during testimony last month. "If waterboarding is torture, torture is not constitutional."

That carefully hedged answer became the central flashpoint of his confirmation process, with Democratic Sens. Chuck Schumer of New York and Dianne Feinstein of California -- both of whom ultimately voted to confirm him -- saying they had received private assurances that Mukasey would enforce any future legal determination that the practice was illegal.

"I did not get the answer I wanted," Schumer said, "but Judge Mukasey convinced me that he has the independence, and the strength of character, to stand up to this administration."

Republicans largely dismissed the controversy as political theater, arguing that discussing classified interrogation methods in public hearings was inappropriate.

"The Justice Department needs a leader now," said Sen. Arlen Specter, R-Pennsylvania. "We cannot leave this critical post vacant over a hypothetical question about a program most senators know only what they read in the newspapers."

The debate unfolded against the backdrop of a new national poll suggesting the American public remains deeply divided over the use of waterboarding in terrorism interrogations.

According to survey results released this week, 51 percent of respondents said the technique should never be used on terrorism suspects, while 40 percent said it could be justified under certain circumstances, such as when a suspect is believed to have information about an imminent attack.

The poll also found a sharp partisan split: 58 percent of Republicans said waterboarding could sometimes be justified, compared with just 28 percent of Democrats. Independents were closely divided.

When asked directly whether waterboarding constitutes torture, 69 percent of those surveyed said yes, while 24 percent said no.

White House officials have repeatedly declined to confirm or deny whether the CIA currently uses waterboarding, citing the need to protect classified intelligence methods. Bush has said only that the United States "does not torture," without addressing specific techniques.

Human rights groups condemned the Senate's decision to confirm Mukasey without a firmer commitment on the issue.

"The Senate just confirmed an attorney general who won't say waterboarding is torture," said Anthony Romero, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union. "That should trouble every American, regardless of party."

Mukasey is expected to be sworn in within days, succeeding Alberto Gonzales, who resigned in September amid separate controversies over the firing of U.S. attorneys and the department's handling of terrorism surveillance programs.

In a statement following the vote, Bush called Mukasey "a brilliant legal mind" and said he was confident the new attorney general would "lead the Justice Department with the independence and integrity the American people deserve."

Mukasey is scheduled to be sworn in at the White House later this week.
